lessons.title: The Kelly Formula for Simple Bets: f* = Edge Divided by Odds

children.text: The previous lesson derived f* = p − q, the optimal bet fraction when a win pays exactly what a loss costs. Almost nothing in real trading pays even money. Lesson 1.2 showed a Bank Nifty options seller winning small and losing bigger, and a Nifty swing trader winning big and losing small. This lesson repeats the same derivation with a general payoff ratio and arrives at the formula the rest of this course uses.

Keep everything from Lesson 2.1 except the payoff. A win still happens with probability p and a loss with probability q = 1 − p, but a win now pays b times the amount staked, where b is the payoff ratio from Lesson 1.2. Betting a fraction f of current capital, the growth rate per trade becomes:

body.caption: A win multiplies capital by (1 + bf); a loss multiplies it by (1 − f)

body.latex: pb(1-f) = q(1+bf) \;\Rightarrow\; pb - q = bf(p+q) = bf \;\Rightarrow\; f^{*} = \dfrac{pb - q}{b}
body.caption: The same (p + q) = 1 simplification used in Lesson 2.1 applies here too

children.text: The same concavity argument from Lesson 2.1 carries over unchanged: g(f) is a sum of two logarithms of positive linear functions of f, which is concave, so this critical point is again the global maximum, not just a candidate.
The Kelly Formula: Edge Divided by Odds

The numerator, pb − q, is exactly the expectancy E(R) defined in Lesson 1.2: the average result per rupee risked. This formula is traditionally summarized as "edge divided by odds," where odds means the payoff ratio b from Lesson 1.2, not the gambling-style "3 to 1" phrasing this course avoids.

body.caption: Three equivalent ways to write the Kelly Criterion for a simple win/lose bet

body.text: Sanity check against Lesson 2.1: set b = 1 and f* = (p·1 − q)/1 = p − q, exactly the even-money formula already derived. The even-money case was never a separate rule. It is this formula with b = 1.

children.text: Applying It to Chapter 1's Two Archetypes
Lesson 1.2 worked out p and b for both archetypes without a sizing formula to plug them into. Now there is one.

body.caption: Kelly fraction for both archetypes from Lesson 1.2

body.title: Optimal fraction f* across three archetypes

children.text: Two very different trading styles land within a percentage point of each other, around 20% of capital. The scalper on the right, introduced in the exercise below, comes out even higher. That is not a coincidence to celebrate. All three numbers are aggressive, and Chapter 3 spends its entire length explaining why almost nobody should actually bet full Kelly, however cleanly it comes out of the algebra.

body.title: Size a high-win-rate scalper
body.prompt: A scalping system wins 85% of the time, with an average win of 0.30x the average loss (b = 0.30). What is f* as a percentage? Round to the nearest whole percent.
body.explanation: E(R) = pb − q = (0.85 × 0.30) − 0.15 = 0.255 − 0.15 = 0.105R. f* = 0.105 ÷ 0.30 = 0.35, or 35%. A very high win rate can justify a large Kelly fraction even when each individual win is small relative to the occasional loss, because losses happen rarely enough that the formula tolerates a bigger bet.

children.text: How f* Moves as the Payoff Ratio Changes
Hold the win rate fixed at 40%, the Nifty swing trader's number, and vary only the payoff ratio, using f* = p − q/b.

body.caption: Fixed p = 0.40, varying payoff ratio b

cells: Negative: no genuine edge, so no bet at all
The Nifty swing trader's actual number
Bigger payoff ratio, bigger Kelly fraction
Approaching p = 0.40 as b grows very large

body.text: A negative f* is not a strategy the formula wants sized small. It is the formula saying this bet has no edge and should not be taken, at any size. Never floor a negative Kelly result at some small positive number; floor it at zero.

body.title: Reading the b-sensitivity table
body.question: In the table above, why does f* increase as b increases, with p held fixed at 40%?
options: Because a larger payoff ratio always means a higher win rate
Because the q/b term shrinks as b grows, so less of the win rate gets subtracted away
Because the formula stops being valid once b exceeds 2
It doesn't actually increase; the table contains an error
body.explanation: f* = p − q/b. As b grows, q/b shrinks toward zero, so f* rises toward p itself. A bigger payoff ratio means losses matter less relative to the size of a typical win, which the formula rewards with a larger optimal fraction, even though p never changes.

cards.definition: f* = (pb − q) / b, the fraction of capital that maximizes long-run growth for a bet with win probability p and payoff ratio b.
pb − q, the expected result per rupee risked. Identical to the expectancy E(R) defined in Lesson 1.2.
The payoff ratio b: this course's term for average win divided by average loss, not gambling-style "3 to 1" notation.
An equivalent form of the Kelly formula, useful for seeing how a bigger payoff ratio raises the optimal fraction for a fixed win rate.

points: f* = (pb − q) / b is the Kelly Criterion for any simple win/lose bet with payoff ratio b, and reduces to f* = p − q when b = 1.
The numerator, pb − q, is exactly the expectancy E(R) from Lesson 1.2. Kelly sizing is expectancy divided by payoff ratio.
A negative f* means the bet has no edge and should be sized at zero, never floored at some small positive number.
Holding win rate fixed, a larger payoff ratio produces a larger Kelly fraction, because losses matter less relative to wins.
Full Kelly fractions computed from realistic p and b are often surprisingly large, frequently 20% or more of capital, which is precisely why Chapter 3 exists.

body.text: f* here is the growth-maximizing fraction under an idealized model with known, fixed p and b. It is not a recommendation to size any real trade this aggressively. Chapter 3 covers why fractional Kelly, not full Kelly, is the practical standard. This lesson is for education only and is not investment or trading advice.
